neutral_facts.value: The prosecution case was that the deceased had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. On the date of the incident, the deceased, his wife, and his daughters were present in the house. The accused persons, including the brother of the deceased and the appellant, entered the house. The appellant was holding an iron rod and inflicted a blow on the head of the deceased. The brother of the deceased gave a lathi blow on other parts of the body of the deceased. Other accused also inflicted lathi blows on the deceased's back. Injuries were also inflicted on the deceased's wife. The accused persons then ran away. The injured were taken to the hospital. The Head Constable recorded the statement of the deceased, which was later treated as a dying declaration. The deceased died in the hospital after a few days. The case was converted into one under Section 302 IPC. The trial court found that the head injury attributed to the appellant was sufficient to cause the death of the deceased and convicted the appellant under Sections 148, 149, 323, 506, 452, and 302 IPC. The High Court refused to interfere with the trial court's order.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the deceased had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. The accused, including the brother of the deceased and the appellant, attacked the deceased, with the appellant inflicting a blow on the head with an iron rod. The deceased's statement, recorded by the Head Constable, was treated as a dying declaration and was found to be clear and satisfactory, corroborated by medical evidence. The prosecution maintained that the deceased's statement was reliable and that the appellant's actions led to the deceased's death.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the statement recorded by the Head Constable was not reliable as a dying declaration, as it should have been recorded by a Magistrate. They also contended that the son and daughter of the deceased were not examined as witnesses, and the findings were based on no evidence. The defence further argued that the conviction should have been under Section 304 (Part II) IPC and not under Section 302 IPC.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that a dying declaration is admissible under Section 32 of the Evidence Act if it is made by a person as to the cause of his death or such circumstances. The Court also considered the intention of the accused and whether the act was committed with the intention to kill or with knowledge that it was likely to cause death.
